Aperol vs. Campari: What’s the Difference?

by Melanie Tornroth | Aug 20, 2026 | Bar Ingredients, Better Bartending, Product Reviews | 0 comments

by Melanie Tornroth | Aug 20, 2026 | Bar Ingredients, Better Bartending, Product Reviews | 0 comments

Copyright A Bar Above, generated with AI

Instaread

 

If you’ve spent any time exploring Italian cocktails– or even if you’ve just enjoyed the ever popular Aperol Spritz and the Negroni– you’ve probably encountered two very colorful bottles: Aperol and Campari. They’re both bittersweet Italian aperitifs, they’re both associated with pre-dinner drinking culture, and they’re even owned by the same parent company today.

So, is Aperol the same as Campari?

The surprising answer: Nope! While they belong to the same general family and can sometimes play similar roles in cocktails, Aperol and Campari are distinctly different in flavor, alcohol content, color, intensity, and history.

When it comes to Aperol vs. Campari, I tend to think of Aperol as the softer, more citrus-forward option and Campari as its bolder, more bitter counterpart. That difference matters quite a bit once you start mixing with them. Personally, I much prefer Aperol, as it’s definitely less aggressive in its flavor profile. But that said, Campari sure has it’s place, and a Negroni with Aperol hits a bit different than the original.

So let’s compare the two Italian aperitifs, including what they taste like, where they come from, their alcohol content, and whether you can actually substitute Aperol for Campari and vice versa.

Photo by Federica Ariemma via www.unsplash.com

Photo by Julia Solonina via www.unsplash.com

 

What is Amaro?

Before comparing Aperol and Campari, it helps to understand the broader world they belong to: amaro.

Amaro is Italian for “bitter,” and the term refers to a broad category of bittersweet herbal liqueurs traditionally enjoyed as aperitifs or digestifs. They’re typically made by infusing alcohol with some combination of herbs, roots, spices, citrus peels, flowers, and other botanicals, then adding sweetness to balance all that bitterness.

And it’s a pretty broad category in terms of how they taste. One amaro might taste bright and citrusy, while another can be intensely herbal, earthy, spicy, or almost medicinal. Alcohol content and sweetness can vary quite a bit, too.

So, are Aperol and Campari amari? Broadly speaking, yes: Both belong to the Italian tradition of bitter, botanical liqueurs. More specifically, they’re commonly described as aperitivo bitters because they’re closely associated with the pre-dinner aperitivo tradition.

That distinction helps explain why Aperol and Campari can seem so similar at first glance without actually being interchangeable. Think of “amaro” as a big family rather than a single flavor profile; these are two rather different members of that same family (probably like you and one of your siblings).

Photo by Janesca via www.unsplash.com

Aperol vs. Campari at a Glance

Aperol and Campari have enough in common that the confusion between them makes total sense. Both are Italian aperitifs with proprietary recipes built around botanical ingredients, and both balance sweetness with bitterness.

But put them side by side, and the differences are pretty obvious:

Copyright A Bar Above, created with AI technologies

 

So while you might see Aperol v. Campari presented as a battle between nearly identical ingredients, they’re really two different approaches to the Italian aperitivo.

Aperol is typically more approachable if you’re new to bitter flavors, while Campari brings significantly more bitterness and alcoholic strength. Aperol itself describes its flavor as citrus-led and slightly floral, with orange zest and a touch of vanilla, while describing Campari as comparatively more bitter.

Photo by Rick Content Studio via www.unsplash.com

 

How to Use Aperol and Campari

Both Aperol and Campari belong naturally in the world of aperitivo, the Italian tradition of enjoying a drink—often alongside small bites—before a meal. And both are fantastic cocktail ingredients but bring their own spirit to the table.

Photo by Victoria Shes via www.unsplash.com

 

Aperol and Campari may look similar on a cocktail spec, but switching between them can substantially change the drink.

Aperol works especially well when you want bitterness without letting it dominate the cocktail. Its lower proof and citrus-forward character make it a natural partner for sparkling wine, soda water, citrus, and lighter spirits. If I want a placebo drink at night, for instance, I’ll add a splash of Aperol to a flavored seltzer; it’s a great, very low-ABV cocktail.

Campari can stand up to much stronger flavors. It’s at home alongside gin and sweet vermouth in a Negroni, bourbon or rye in a Boulevardier, or simply soda water for a refreshing highball. You may want to adjust the amount you use if you’re adding some to a sparkling water for your own, more bitter version of an amaro-soda spritz like what I described above.

Neither one is better; they’re just different!

Photo by Olena Bohovyk via www.unsplash.com

 

History of Aperol and Campari

Campari is the elder of the two by nearly 60 years.

Gaspare Campari created his namesake bitter in 1860. The brand became closely associated with Milan, where Gaspare eventually operated Caffè Campari in the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II. In 1915, his son Davide opened Camparino in the Galleria, further connecting Campari with Milanese aperitivo culture. The most famous cocktails with Campari are the Negroni and the Americano (not to be confused with the coffee drink).

Aperol came along in 1919, created by brothers Luigi and Silvio Barbieri in Padua after seven years of experimentation. It subsequently became particularly popular around Padua and Venice. Today, it’s best known for the Aperol Spritz, of course.

The familiar Aperol Spritz formula emerged in the 1950s and eventually helped turn the orange aperitif into an international symbol of Italian-style social drinking.

Although their stories began separately, today both brands sit within the Campari Group portfolio. As I mentioned, their shared ownership doesn’t mean they’re the same product, though, and their individual recipes remain distinct.

Copyright A Bar Above, generated with AI

 

Aperol vs. Campari: Ingredients and Flavor

This is where the Campari vs. Aperol comparison becomes much more interesting.

Both recipes are proprietary, so we can’t simply compare complete ingredient lists. We can, however, look at the flavors and botanicals that their producers disclose.

Photo by James Jeremy Beckers via www.unsplash.com

 

What Does Aperol Taste Like?

Aperol is distinctly citrus-forward.

The brand identifies citrus peel and citrus oils alongside aromatic herbs, roots, and woods as components contributing to its character. It also identifies orange and cinchona as dominant flavors, while gentian is another disclosed botanical.

In the glass, expect:

  • Sweet and bitter orange
  • Citrus zest
  • Herbal notes
  • A hint of vanilla
  • Gentle root-like bitterness
  • A lingering bittersweet finish

There is definitely bitterness here, but it’s rounded by sweetness and bright citrus.

That’s one reason Aperol can be a good introduction to bitter aperitifs if you haven’t developed a taste for more assertively bitter amari yet.

Photo by Alex Reynolds via www.unsplash.com

 

What Does Campari Taste Like?

Campari takes bitterness several steps further.

Its exact recipe is famously guarded, but its signature character is unmistakably bitter, herbal, and complex. The stronger bitter backbone is precisely why Campari works so well in drinks containing other flavorful ingredients, meaning it doesn’t disappear very easily.

Compared directly with Aperol, Campari generally tastes less sweet and more intensely bitter. And that difference isn’t subtle.

If you make two otherwise identical drinks, one with Aperol and one with Campari, you’re likely to notice a significant shift in the balance of the cocktail.

Photo by Gabriella Clare Marino via www.unsplash.com

 

Is Aperol Sweeter Than Campari?

Yes, at least perceptually because of the other ingredients and balance of everything together.

Aperol’s bright citrus, vanilla notes, gentler bitterness, and lower alcoholic intensity create a softer and sweeter overall impression. Campari’s stronger bitter character makes it taste considerably drier and more aggressive by comparison.

This is one of the most important things to consider when deciding which bottle belongs in your cocktail.

Copyright A Bar Above, generated with AI

 

Aperol vs. Campari Alcohol Content

Another major difference between Aperol and Campari is their strength.

In the United States, Aperol is 11% ABV. Aperol’s own U.S. materials list Campari at 25% ABV, making Campari more than twice the alcoholic volume. That gap affects more than how strong the final drink is. But remember that a spirit like whiskey, vodka, or gin is generally 35-40%, so both amari are still lower in ABV than a traditional liquor.

Alcohol carries aroma and flavor, so Campari’s higher proof contributes to its bigger presence in a cocktail. Aperol, meanwhile, is particularly well suited to lower-ABV drinks and tall, sparkling drinks.

Of course, the alcohol content of the finished cocktail depends on every ingredient and the proportions used. An Aperol Spritz isn’t automatically a low-alcohol drink simply because Aperol itself has a lower ABV, so it’s always worth keeping the entire recipe and serving size in mind.

Photo by Riccardo Andolfo via www.unsplash.com

 

Can You Substitute Aperol for Campari?

Technically, yes. But I wouldn’t call them equal substitutes.

Swapping Aperol for Campari will generally make a cocktail less bitter, less alcoholic, more citrus-forward, and softer overall. Replacing Aperol with Campari does essentially the opposite: You’ll introduce substantially more bitterness, proof, and intensity. It’s best to think of it as a variation rather than a one-for-one replacement.

Copyright A Bar Above

 

Take the Negroni. Its classic structure depends on the bold bitterness of Campari balancing gin and sweet vermouth. Replace the Campari with Aperol, and you’ll still have a perfectly drinkable cocktail… But it won’t taste like a classic Negroni.

Likewise, replacing Aperol with Campari in an Aperol Spritz creates a considerably more bitter drink known aptly as the Campari Spritz. As you already know, it isn’t my personal preference, but a lot of people love it more than the traditional Aperol version. It’s simply a different cocktail experience and definitely depends on your own taste buds.

When we’re developing or testing recipes, Chris is always thinking about balance rather than simply whether two ingredients occupy the same category. That’s a useful approach at home, too: When you substitute one bitter aperitif for another, taste the whole drink and adjust accordingly.

Copyright A Bar Above

 

Variations and Cocktails to Try

But don’t take my word at face value. I think it’s pretty obvious I have a little bias here! Honestly, the easiest way to understand the difference between Aperol and Campari is to actually just taste them one after the other.

Try a small amount of each on its own first. Then add soda water and taste again. Dilution can reveal aromas and flavors that are harder to identify when you’re concentrating exclusively on the bitterness. After that, start mixing.

Aperol is a natural choice for:

  • Aperol Spritz
  • Paper Plane
  • Naked and Famous
  • Aperol Sour
  • Aperol and soda
  • Lighter spritz variations

Copyright A Bar Above

 

Campari is traditional in:

  • Negroni
  • Boulevardier
  • Americano
  • Jungle Bird
  • Campari and soda
  • Campari Spritz

Copyright A Bar Above

 

Our Variation: Swap and Compare

For a simple home experiment, make the same basic spritz twice: one version with Aperol and another with Campari. Keep your sparkling wine, soda, ice, glassware, and proportions consistent so that the bitter aperitif is the only major variable. Taste them side-by-side.

The Aperol version should emphasize citrus, sweetness, and gentler bitterness. The Campari version should be deeper, more bitter, and stronger.

This isn’t necessarily about deciding which one is “better.” It’s about learning what each ingredient contributes to a cocktail; side-by-side tasting is one of the easiest ways to train your palate and decide which you prefer (or if you love both for their own qualities).

Copyright A Bar Above, generated with AI

 

Two Italian Icons, Two Very Different Bottles

So, are Aperol and Campari the same? Definitely not.

As we’ve talked about, they’re related stylistically: Both are Italian bittersweet aperitifs with deep ties to aperitivo culture. But their similarities shouldn’t overshadow what makes each bottle distinctive.

Aperol is bright orange, citrus-forward, gently bittersweet, and relatively low in alcohol at 11% ABV. Campari is deep red, significantly more bitter and intense, and substantially higher in alcohol– although still low compared to spirits like vodka or rum.

If you enjoy lighter, fruitier, and less bitter cocktails, start with Aperol. If you love assertive bitterness and classics like the Negroni, Campari deserves a permanent place on your bar cart. And if you like both? Even better. They’re different enough that I don’t consider owning both redundant.

Photo by Dogu Tuncer via www.unsplash.com

 

Learning the distinction between Aperol vs. Campari is also a great example of why understanding ingredients matters in mixology. Two bottles can occupy a similar category without doing the same job, and figuring out exactly what each contributes is part of the fun of becoming a better home bartender.

I’m curious what you think and which you prefer… If you even have a preference, that is. Leave me a comment below and let me know!
